title: How to Choose Foil for Coated Art Paper Packaging

seo.title: How to Choose Foil for Coated Art Paper Packaging

content:
Coated art paper is widely used in cosmetic boxes, gift boxes, retail cartons and premium printed packaging. Its smooth surface can create a bright metallic result, but it can also make defects more visible if the foil or process setting is not suitable.

## Why Coated Art Paper Needs Careful Foil Selection

The smooth coating helps the foil sit cleanly on the surface. This is good for high-gloss gold, silver and rose gold effects. At the same time, smooth paper can show pinholes, pressure marks, cloudy areas or edge problems more clearly than rough paper.

If the paper is already printed, the ink system becomes important. A foil may stamp well on blank coated paper but perform differently on printed ink, UV coating or protective varnish. Always approve the foil on the real printed sheet.

## What to Check Before Buying

For coated art paper packaging, buyers should check four things: brightness, edge clarity, adhesion and batch color consistency. Premium boxes often require the same gold tone across multiple production runs, so color approval should be based on a stamped sample, not only a roll or color card.

If the design includes fine text and large solid areas, test both. Fine text checks the clarity of the transfer. Solid areas reveal coverage and gloss stability.

## Practical Testing Advice

Stamp the foil on blank coated paper and the actual printed sheet. Compare the result. If the foil works on blank paper but peels or looks dull on the printed sheet, the top surface may need a more compatible foil grade.

After stamping, run tape, rub and folding tests. For cosmetic packaging, also consider scratch resistance because boxes are handled often during filling, transport and display.

## FAQ

### Why does coated paper show pinholes?

Pinholes may come from dust, uneven pressure, surface contamination, unsuitable foil coverage or unstable feeding.

### Can one foil work on printed and unprinted coated paper?

Sometimes, but both surfaces should be tested because ink and varnish can change adhesion.
